subject: system-design
question: In an eventually consistent system, what is guaranteed if no new writes occur?
options: All replicas eventually converge to the same value
Writes are rejected while replicas synchronize
Replicas never diverge, even while writes are in flight
Every read immediately returns the latest write
explanation: Eventual consistency promises convergence over time, not immediate agreement on every read.

subject: system-design
question: How does an ETag or version field prevent lost updates?
options: The update succeeds only if the version still matches what the client last read
It forces every read to hit the primary
It encrypts the record so only one client can read it
It deletes the old record after each update
explanation: This is optimistic concurrency control; a mismatch returns a conflict so the client can re-read and retry.

subject: system-design
question: What is optimistic concurrency control?
options: Locking every row before reading it
Allowing all writes and keeping the first one
Proceeding without locks and checking for conflicts at commit, retrying if data changed
Running transactions one at a time
explanation: It works well when conflicts are rare, since no locks are held while work is done.

subject: system-design
question: Which guarantee means a user always sees their own previous updates?
options: Last-writer-wins merging
Linearizability across all clients
Exactly-once delivery
Read-your-writes consistency
explanation: Read-your-writes is a session guarantee; it can be met by routing a user's reads to the primary or to a replica that has their write.

subject: system-design
question: What is the main risk of last-write-wins conflict resolution?
options: Concurrent updates can silently overwrite each other, and clock skew can pick the wrong winner
It requires a global lock on every write
It makes reads impossible during replication
It requires all writes to go through a single leader
explanation: LWW keeps one value and discards the others, so a legitimate concurrent update can be lost.

subject: system-design
question: What does strong consistency guarantee for reads?
options: Reads are always served from a local cache
Reads may return any previously written value
Every read returns the most recent committed write
Reads never fail during a network partition
explanation: Strongly consistent systems behave as if there were a single up-to-date copy, often at a cost in latency or availability.

subject: system-design
question: Which consistency model is weaker than linearizability but still preserves cause-and-effect ordering?
options: Serializability without any ordering
Causal consistency
Exactly-once processing
Read uncommitted
explanation: Causal consistency keeps causally related operations in order, while concurrent operations may be seen in different orders.
